newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British Business - July 28th 1997.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British Business - July 28th 1997.

text.p: This daily press summary is produced for Reuters by the Broadcast Monitoring Company, which is responsible for its contents. For further information on these articles or details of BMC's other international press and broadcast services call Simon McMillan on "44 (0)171 256 5130 or e-mail bmc.co@ft.com
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- BBC TALKS WITH BSKYB ON BRINK OF FAILURE

Talks between BSkyB and the BBC concerning digital transmission of its programmes by satellite are set to reach an inconclusive end, as BSkyB are seeking a fee 300m stg more than the BBC is willing to pay. BSkyB operates the only satellite capable of broadcasting BBC programmes, and believes carrying the programming of such a major company will make Oftel regulators less concerned about its monopoly. It is possible Oftel may intervene in the talks to help them reach a favourable conclusion.
-- NEWSPAPER BODY ISSUES COPYRIGHT WRIT AGAINST M&S

The Newspaper Licensing Agency has initiated legal action against Marks & Spencer for refusing to purchase a licence which permits it to copy and fax newspaper articles. The Agency claims M&S make over 250,000 newspaper photocopies per year and distributes them to staff without the 80 pound stg licence authorising the process. A request has been made to the courts seeking an injunction against the making or transmitting of future illegal copies.
-- CORTECS APPOINTS JAPANESE DEALER

Biotechnology group Cortecs International has signed a partnership with Japan's Zeria Pharmaceuticals which will permit it to sell its pioneering blood test to detect the Helicobacter Pylori bacterium, the major cause of gastric ulcers. Zeria has 500 salesmen and holds a ten per cent share of the 2.4bn stg Japanese peptic ulcer treatments market. Cortecs has also announced the launch of its new osteoporosis test Osteosal would be delayed until later this year.
THE TIMES
-- BT FACES MORE PRESSURE

British Telecoms' investors are expected to increase their pressure on the UK telecoms giant this week to outline its new terms for the planned takeover of US long-distance carrier MCI. It is expected investors will demand a renegotiation of the deal in the wake of MCI's profit warning earlier in the month. MCI will release its second-quarter figures on Wednesday, while BT's first-quarter results will come on Thursday.
-- VIRGIN COLA AIMS TO BURST PEPSI BUBBLE

Following sessions with leading UK supermarket chains such as Asda, Safeway and Somerfield, Virgin Cola - the company owned by Richard Branson and Canada's Cotts - will double the number of retail outlets carrying the drink this summer. The move increases Virgin's sales from 30 per cent of the market to 60 per cent, enabling the cola to better compete with Pepsi and Coke. J Sainsbury has refused to stock the drink, looking to increase sales of its own.
-- ENERGY FIRMS SCALE BACK EFFICIENCY COMMITMENTS

Figures compiled for The Times newspaper show energy groups in the UK are cutting back on their commitments to efficiency, with many only adhering to the minimum amount set out by the National Energy Action. In 1995, companies paid 721,000 stg for consultancy on energy efficiency, but in the current financial year the NEA estimates payments of below 500,000 stg with Midlands and Midlands Energy accounting for the largest contributions - a combined 412,500 stg.
THE GUARDIAN
-- BLAIR TO SEND DAVID SAINSBURY TO THE OTHER PLACE

Tony Blair has appointed three leading businessmen as life peers in the House of Lords in an attempt to increase the number of Labour members so that they counterbalance the Tory members. The three new appointees are J Sainsbury chairman David Sainsbury, Andrew Stone, the joint managing director of Marks & Spencer and George Simpson, managing director of GEC.
-- CITY EXPECTS 675M STG PROFIT FROM ABBEY NATIONAL

Former building society Abbey National, the first such group to convert to a bank, will release its first-half results on Tuesday. Abbey, rumoured to be in partnership talks with National Westminster Bank, is expected to reveal pre-tax profits of 675m stg.
-- SAGA AIMS FOR 'WHITE' PRICE

Senior citizens travel and financial services group Saga has declared its intention to enter the 'white goods' market, as it is currently in talks with a major intermediary firm to supply the over four million Saga customers with household appliances at a discount price. Prices at Saga could be as much as 15 per cent lower than those of high street retailers and its electrical retail arm will open at the same time as the department of Trade & Industry releases its report into high street price fixing.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- RETAILERS QUEUE UP TO JOIN THE EXODUS TO OUT-OF-TOWN SITES

A report published by retail analyst Verdict predicts that by 2001, out- of-town stores will account for over 33 per cent of retail sales, as the number of outlets rises 25 per cent to over 6,000. Presently, the superstores account for 29 per cent of sales, and were accountable for over half of the 8.4bn increase in retail sales for 1996.
-- SKY SET TO 'UNBUNDLE' DISNEY CHANNEL

Subsequent to an Independent Television Commission ruling that the 'bundling' of television channels was anti-competitive, BSkyB is to announce customers looking to subscribe to the Disney Channel will no longer have to subscribe to two other channels as well. While the majority of the public agree with the 'anti-bundling' stance, some wonder how much interest Disney will attract on its own, and Flextech Television chief Brent Harman states if all channels were offered 'a la carte, it would ruin channel economics and be an administrative nightmare'.
-- BA STAKE IN RESERVATIONS SYSTEM VALUED AT $308M

British Airways has affirmed its stake in World-wide airline computer reservations group Galileo will be valued at $308m by a New York flotation. BA is to retain seven per cent ($171m) of the business unless demand dictates it release more shares under the terms of the float and the public offering will value Galileo $2.45bn. BA, meanwhile, announced it had not yet been approached by the EU on reports competition commissioner Karel van Miert was looking for it to make massive cuts in transatlant ic flight costs as compensation for clearing the American Airlines link-up.
